column3: You have written down the three workflows that must work on day one.
column4: "Everything" is not a scope. Three workflows can be tested; everything cannot.

column3: You know who owns the data on your side.
column4: Migration stalls the first time nobody can say which of three rates is right.
column5: One named person for masters, one for projects, one for balances.

column3: You have asked what is included in onboarding and what is chargeable.
column4: Implementation cost is where quoted price and final invoice usually part company.
column5: Get it in writing: migration, training sessions, configuration, support period.

column3: You know what happens to your existing accounting system.
column4: Most contractors keep their accounting software. Find out whether it is a migration or an ongoing integration — they are very different promises.
column5: Ask specifically: one-time import, or continuous two-way sync?

column3: You have agreed what 'go-live' means and who signs it off.
column4: Without acceptance criteria, a rollout has no end and the spreadsheets never stop.
column5: A short written list: these workflows, running in the system, signed by these people.

column2: Masters — where the work actually is
column3: Item master is de-duplicated before import.
column4: The same cable in four spellings at three rates produces confident, wrong reporting forever.
column5: Sort your item list alphabetically and read it. You will find them.

column2: Masters — where the work actually is
column3: Vendor master has GSTIN, PAN and bank details, with dead vendors removed.
column4: Importing dead vendors carries a decade of noise into a clean system.
column5: Vendors with no transaction in 24 months.

column2: Masters — where the work actually is
column3: Labour and subcontract rate masters reflect current signed contracts.
column4: Bills will be checked against these rates. Wrong rates are worse than no rates.
column5: Spot-check ten rates against the actual work orders.

column2: Masters — where the work actually is
column3: Cost heads and BOQ structure are agreed before anything is imported.
column4: Changing the structure after data is in is the most expensive rework in any rollout.
column5: One page: how you want to see cost, and whether reports can produce it.

column2: Masters — where the work actually is
column3: Users and their roles are listed, including site staff.
column4: Role design decides whether site staff actually use the system or work around it.
column5: Who raises, who approves, who sees money. Write it as a table.

column3: Running projects are migrated with their BOQs, not just new ones.
column4: If only new projects go in, two systems run in parallel and one of them wins — usually the spreadsheet.
column5: Count your live projects. All of them should appear in the plan.

column3: Work already executed on those projects is brought in as opening position.
column4: Otherwise the first RA bill from the new system is wrong, and trust is lost in week one.
column5: Cumulative quantity billed per project, as at the cut-off date.

column3: Opening receivables, payables and retention held are entered and agreed.
column4: Without them the first month's cash view is fiction.
column5: Tie the totals to your books at the cut-off date, and have your accountant sign it.

column3: Open advances with subcontractors and vendors are carried over.
column4: An advance that does not migrate is an advance nobody recovers.
column5: Ledger of open advances at cut-off.

column3: A cut-off date is fixed, and everyone knows what happens either side of it.
column4: Ambiguity about the cut-off produces double entry and missing entry at once.
column5: One date, written down, communicated to site and office.

column3: Training is by role and uses your own data, not a demo company.
column4: Generic training does not survive contact with a real site.
column5: Separate sessions for site staff and office staff, on your migrated projects.

column3: Site staff can do their part on the phone they already have.
column4: If the field cannot file from a phone, the data stops at the office and the system becomes a reporting burden.
column5: Have one site engineer file a daily report during the demo, on their own handset.

column3: A parallel-run period is defined — and has an end date.
column4: Parallel running without an end date is how a rollout quietly becomes permanent duplication.
column5: Two to four weeks is typical. Write the end date down.

column3: Acceptance criteria are tested and signed before the old way stops.
column4: This is the moment the rollout either lands or drifts.
column5: Each agreed workflow demonstrated end to end, signed by the person who owns it.

column3: You know who to call, and what the support arrangement is.
column4: The first month generates more questions than the next year.
column5: Named contact, hours, channel, and what counts as chargeable.

column3: You have a rollback position if go-live fails.
column4: Rarely needed, and the day you need it you will need it badly.
column5: Your exported data, and the date until which the old system stays available.
